title: Appearance
subtitle: What the eye can conclude
objectives: Assess clarity, intensity and colour precisely
Use colour to estimate age and grape

steps.title: A precise scale
steps.body: Systematic tasting uses fixed words so notes can be compared. Clarity: clear or hazy. Intensity: pale, medium or deep. Colour: for whites, lemon-green, lemon, gold, amber or brown; for rosés, pink, salmon or orange; for reds, purple, ruby, garnet, tawny or brown. Look at the core and the rim separately.
steps.highlight: Clear or hazy; pale, medium, deep

steps.title: Reading the evidence
steps.body: Deep colour in a young red suggests thick skins, like Syrah or Cabernet, or a warm climate. Pale colour suggests Pinot Noir, Grenache or Nebbiolo. A wide watery rim in a red shows age. In whites, gold can mean age, oak or sweetness; amber or brown suggests oxidation or deliberate oxidative ageing, as in Oloroso.
steps.highlight: Colour hints at grape, climate and age

steps.prompt: A young red is deep purple and nearly opaque. Which grape is most likely?
steps.explanation: Syrah's thick skins give deep, dark colour. Pinot Noir, Nebbiolo and Grenache are all naturally paler.

steps.title: Faults you can see
steps.body: Haze in a wine that should be clear can mean a protein or microbial problem, though some unfiltered wines are naturally slightly cloudy. Bubbles in a still wine may mean refermentation in bottle. Brown tones in a young white suggest oxidation. Tartrate crystals and red sediment are harmless.
steps.highlight: Haze or browning can warn of faults

steps.prompt: A gold colour in a white wine always means the wine is old.
steps.explanation: Not true. Gold can come from age, but also from oak ageing, a warm climate, sweetness or long skin contact. Look for other clues.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Use fixed terms for clarity, intensity and colour
Deep colour suggests thick skins or warmth; pale suggests thin skins
Haze, browning or bubbles in a still wine can signal a fault
